Okay, you hit a lot of points here, so let's go through them. I'll start off by saying that we view the minimum wage very differently, as you view it as forcing people to pay more, and I view it as increasing the amount people get paid. I'll point out again that the studies for McDonalds showed something like a 4% price increase for raising the wages to $15 an hour, while almost doubling the employees rate of pay. I think most people would be thrilled to double their paycheck and see only 4% increased costs. But let's move on to the points you made:

Going after money in the ground. Ahh, "Drill baby drill.", I shouldn't have been surprised. Let's look at how the different energy sectors are doing:

Oil Let's start with the big one, oil. Oil and gasoline run everything, but it's not a good growth industry right now. The price of oil is in freefall, and multiple sources are pointing out that it could drop as low as $20 a barrel in the near future. Not exactly great prospects for creating new jobs or mending a sluggish economy. In fact, here's one of the more recent reports from Goldman: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JskY8n6sTHA

Natural Gas Natural gas is having a boom right now, and we've got so much of it that we've run out of places to store the stuff. That would be great for exporting, except for one major flaw. This huge boom in natural gas is the result of fracking, and it's recently been discovered that a fracking well is only a strong producer for up to 3 years, instead of around 10 years as was originally expected. This means that most fracking wells are in fact, unprofitable in the long term. Here's an article that discusses that: http://fortune.com/2015/01/09/oil-prices-shale-fracking/

Coal We can't ignore coal, of course. The dirtiest of all the energy sources. The idea of "Clean Coal" has been debunked, and it's well known that particulate pollution, the kind that coal is most known for, is a serious danger to human health. It causes respiratory and cardiovascular problems and a wealth of environmental processes. For these and other reasons coal has been in sharp decline within this country, and that sinking ship isn't going to be the one to lift the economy. Here's some data to back up coal's decline: http://www.ucsusa.org/sites/default/files/legacy/assets/documents/clean_energy/Ripe-for-Retirement-An-Economic-Analysis-of-the-US-Coal-Fleet.pdf

I will mention that the energybiz.com article you used shows a very poor grasp of science overall, failing to grasp even some of the basics of thermodynamics in ways that are essential to understanding issues such as climate change. If you are relying on their analysis, you are doing yourself a disservice.

With the price of oil plummeting globally exporting gas isn't going to do us a lot of good. In fact, gas prices stopped falling along with the price of oil in the US some months back, and there's a lot to suggest that the price is already being artificially propped up, which makes it even more unsuitable to export.

So, as far as the energy sector, I have to disagree that we need to focus on "going after the money in the ground" I do think the energy sector has a lot to offer as a vehicle to boost the economy, but I think there's a lot more benefit in pushing to expanding the coming renewable-energy infrastructure and being among the first to dominate that market than there is in going after fossil fuels that are increasingly difficult and expensive to obtain. It would be much smarter in the long term for us to become experts in renewable energy and then have that technology to sell and license to the rest of the world. If we don't do it, someone else will and we'll eventually be stuck buying from them or trying to compete with an established market.

I agree fully on bringing back manufacturing, we never should have stopped in the first time. I'd love to see us restore that and make "Made in the USA" a symbol of top quality once again.

On dismantling the Fed, I agree there too. I'd be happy to see them go.
